title: Albertans vote on non-binding separation question Monday
excerpt: Albertans are voting Monday on Question 10, a non-binding referendum item about whether Alberta should begin the legal process for a future separation vote.
body:
Ballots are being counted by hand in Alberta’s referendum, with Question 10 set to be tallied first and results on the separation question expected in the early hours of Tuesday, according to Elections Alberta and BBC News.

Albertans voted Monday on Question 10 of a provincial referendum asking whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada or whether the government should begin the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution for a later binding referendum on separation, according to BBC News and Elections Alberta.

The question is the only choice item on the ballot and is not binding. Elections Alberta says voters will also decide nine other referendum questions, all of them yes-or-no measures. The agency says ballots will be counted by hand and Question 10 will be counted first. BBC reports the count starts no earlier than 8 p.m. local time Monday and that results on the separation question are expected in the early hours of Tuesday.

The official referendum wording reads: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

Premier Danielle Smith has said she opposes separation. The referendum page on Elections Alberta’s site says Alberta has been in a referendum period since March 31, 2026, and that Question 10’s referendum period began May 28.

The separation question reached the ballot after citizen-led petitions pushed the issue into provincial politics. BBC News reported that the pro-separation petition gathered about 300,000 signatures, while a separate petition opposing separation drew more than 400,000. Elections Alberta later validated the pro-separation petition, saying it verified nearly 223,000 signatures out of almost 280,000 valid names counted, according to Global News.

A court blocked the pro-separation petition after finding that First Nations had not been properly consulted, and that ruling is being appealed, BBC News and Global News reported. The Alberta government says that, if the option to begin the process wins, it would start the legal steps needed for a future binding referendum on separation.

On the campaign trail, Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Albertans to reject separation. In a transcript posted by the Prime Minister’s Office of remarks he delivered Friday at the Forever Canadian Rally in Edmonton, Carney said, “Don’t be fooled by the idea you can ‘send a message’ with your vote. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians.”

Polling cited in the reports suggests most Albertans expect the separatist debate to continue even if the vote does not lead to a binding referendum. Fox News reported that an Abacus Data poll of 1,021 respondents released Saturday found 74% of decided voters favored Alberta remaining in Canada, while another Abacus poll found 61% of the 1,021 eligible voters surveyed expected Albertans would vote again on separation even if most chose to remain. Fox also reported that an Angus Reid Institute survey released Friday found 62% of 1,010 Albertans surveyed believed there would never be an end to the separatist movement in the province.

Chris Scott, founder of the pro-separatist group Let’s Talk Alberta, told BBC News on the eve of the vote that the campaign had already accomplished part of its goal. “The key is the conversation has started and it needs to continue,” he said. “What’s started can’t be stopped now,” he added.

Fox News reported that more than 1.2 million Albertans had already cast a ballot as of Saturday.

issues.claim: Ballots are being counted by hand in Alberta’s referendum, with Question 10 set to be tallied first and results on the separation question expected in the early hours of Tuesday, according to Elections Alberta and BBC News.
issues.problem: The sources say the hand count starts no earlier than 8 p.m. local time Monday. The article later says that too. This lead incorrectly presents counting as already underway before the scheduled start time.
issues.fix: Change to future tense, e.g. "Ballots will be counted by hand in Alberta’s referendum..." or "Ballots are to be counted by hand..."

issues.claim: Carney said, “Don’t be fooled by the idea you can ‘send a message’ with your vote. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians.”
issues.problem: The direct quote is not verbatim to the Prime Minister’s Office transcript, which begins "And don’t be fooled..." The article drops the opening word from the quoted passage.
issues.fix: Quote the transcript exactly: "And don’t be fooled by the idea you can ‘send a message’ with your vote. This is not poker..." or paraphrase without quotation marks.

issues.problem: The sentence attributes this quotation to Albertans, but the source does not name that person near the quotation.
issues.fix: Attribute the quotation to the person the source names, or paraphrase.

fc.summary: Most material facts match the source excerpts, but the lead wrongly says ballot counting is already happening before the scheduled start time, and one Carney quotation trims a word from the official transcript.

log.summary: Removed unsupported turnout framing and kept the focus on the official wording, the non-binding status, the petition history and the count timeline. Tightened attribution and separated the prime minister’s remarks to the transcripted Edmonton rally.
